content_voiceover: This page repeats two classic exam themes. Question seven asks which statements about FLT3 mutations are wrong, and three of the four are. FLT3 mutations link to higher peripheral blast counts and a normal karyotype, but not specifically to FAB M1 morphology, so that's wrong. The one true statement is that FLT3 ITD does not affect complete remission rate after standard induction, it mainly drives relapse risk, not induction response. Claiming FLT3 ITD carries higher prognostic significance after age seventy is also wrong, since its impact is generally attenuated in older patients. And the phase three MORPHO trial of gilteritinib maintenance after transplant did not meet its primary endpoint of relapse free survival in the overall population, benefit appeared mainly in patients with detectable measurable residual disease. Question twenty is the familiar therapy related AML item, and the wrong statement again reverses the latency periods, alkylating agents actually cause secondary AML after a longer latency than topoisomerase two inhibitors do.
keypoints: FLT3 mutations link to blast count and normal karyotype, not specifically FAB M1
FLT3-ITD presence does not lower complete remission rate after induction
FLT3-ITD prognostic impact is attenuated, not increased, in patients over seventy
MORPHO trial missed its primary RFS endpoint overall; benefit was in MRD positive patients
Alkylating agents cause AML after a longer latency than topoisomerase two inhibitors
keypoint_voiceover: Key FLT3 facts for boards. FLT3 ITD doesn't change your complete remission rate after induction, it's a relapse risk marker. Its prognostic weight actually shrinks in patients over seventy, it doesn't grow. And the MORPHO trial of gilteritinib maintenance missed its overall relapse free survival endpoint, benefit was confined to MRD positive patients. Finally, keep the t-AML latency straight, alkylating agents take longer to cause leukemia than topoisomerase two inhibitors.
